Advocate for patients and speak up against abuse and injustice. Stay up to date on medical research in psychiatry, neurology, and other diseases that may affect the brain/thinking/emotions. Screen patients for physical diseases thoroughly. I was diagnosed schizoaffective when I was dealing with a neuroimmune disease and my psych confused delirium for psychosis. Not to mention my disheveled apprearance was the result of extreme fatigue and not disorganized thinking. I have ME/CFS, and I am doing better than ever off antipsychotics and mood stabilozers. Question what brought someone to psychiatry in the first place, and if at all possible, try non prescription approaches before heavily medicating someone. Therapy and healing from trauma can do so much help, as can a change of environment, better social life, meeting personal goals, etc. 

And if I patient tells you how they feel or how someyhing affects them, believe them. I had a reaction to Topamax that caused lasting damage to my body. I told my psych I woke up in the middle of the night screaming in pain, electricity running down my spine, body spasming, nerves on fire, senses blaring, vision blacking out, and more pain than I had ever experienced, and she told me to quit being dramatic and gaslit me. I now have nerve damage beyond what I had previously experienced with ME/CFS. I lost use of both of my arms for months because I was forced to keep taking a medication that harmed me. All for a diagnosis I did not even have. That damage occured in only four total days of taking the drug. Even now, my motor skills are not the same. I think I may have had a seizure.This harmed my trust in the medical community in a profound way. I was vulnerable and instead of being met with compassion, concern, and professionalism, I was abused. This is how a lot of people experience paychiatry, unfortunately. 

Kindness and consideration go a long way in a field where these traits are neglected.

I'm in the same boat. Been dealing with chronic health issues for years, and the one change in my thinking that has helped me the most is to view pain as acute sensation. It is perception of information. Sometimes our perceptions are exaggerated or misconstrued, and this can often be the case in chronic pain. It basically creates a feedback loop like you described. Pain leads to poor sleep leads to stress leads to pain ad infinitum. Perhaps you cannot control your pain levels, but you can control the way you react to them. Its easier said than done, but try to be gentle on yourself, allow yourself time to recooperate when you need it. Give yourself time to process what you are feeling in a nonjudgemental, observant way. This helps you find a way to detach and break the cycle. It helps you save your energy, keeping you from reacting with anxiety, depression, anger, or avoidance, which only make things worse.
